title: Teaching History at the Death of History
author: Chris Doyle
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-20-at-12.56.47-PM-680x451.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/teaching-
history-at-the-death-of-history/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-20-at-12.56.47-PM-680x451.png)

Photo by [Mario
Gogh](https://unsplash.com/@mariogogh?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

My subject, history, is in terminal decline. A.I. finally killed it, but it
has been sick since the late twentieth century. The demise of a reading
public, disinformation, fake news, and political spin fatally weakened it.
Undergraduates have fled the history major, and PhDs can’t find jobs teaching
or writing it.[[1]]() It’s curtains for my vocation.

The timing is sadly ironic. We need history. Without it, we’re adrift in a sea
of events without precedent, cause, or meaning. Cut off from the past, we
become prey to those who would use history for nefarious purposes: those who
deny precedents by saying “nothing like this has ever happened before.”[[2]]()
Those who start wars by claiming that its victims “have no history”
independent of the aggressors.[[3]]()Those who twist a deadly riot into a “day
of love.”[[4]]() Orwell was right when he warned that he who controls the past
controls the future. We ignore his words at our peril. There’s tragedy in a
society killing the thing that could save it.

I earned my doctorate in history thirty years ago, just as things began coming
apart. I didn’t see it, then, but paid attention in 1994 when _eminence grise_
historian Eric Hobsbawm prefaced his masterpiece study of the twentieth
century, _The Age of Extremes,_ with the lament “most young men and women at
the century’s end grow up in a sort of permanent present” divorced from
historical events shaping their own moment. Hobsbawm attributed youthful
amnesia to the frenetic pace and news-cycle distortion of modern life.[[5]]()
It was an early warning of an illness that has now progressed beyond the point
of recovery. Here’s why:

Because we’ve ceded our intellectual lives to small screens and small ideas.
This happened “gradually, then suddenly,” to borrow Ernest Hemingway’s quip
about bankruptcy. It’s due to social media and the iPhone, both of which came
into existence in the aughts. The effects of this are dismally catalogued by
Rose Horowitch’s recent essay in _The Atlantic_ proclaiming “The End of
Reading Is Here.”[[6]]() People aren’t illiterate, exactly, but they’ve lost
capacity for the concentration to get through books, and they lack contextual
awareness and vocabularies to make sense of most literature. As goes the
reading public, so goes history.

Because we’ve become cognitively shallow. By design, social media makes us
distracted, outraged, reactive, addicted.[[7]]() We’ve conditioned ourselves
out of the “slow thinking” described by economist Daniel Kahneman.[[8]]() That
sort of thought, deliberative, critical, rational, is the stock-in-trade of
history. It’s painstaking. Practitioners of slow-thinking have been
marginalized as arbiters of cultural truth, replaced by “influencers” dealing
in anger, shock, emotion.

Because, as deliberative thinkers are ushered offstage, we’ve surrendered
their public functions to artificial intelligence. History educators have
resisted A.I. Their approach favors the creation of sterile classroom
environments, scrubbed of A.I., and the confinement of student writing to
policed spaces.[[9]]() I’ve tried this, with some success, but it strikes me
as a stopgap and ultimately futile.

That’s because students, with help from Big Tech, keep getting more savvy
about disguising A.I. plagiarism, which they find irresistible.[[10]]() A
fashionable corollary trend castigates anyone who would deny young people the
benefits of A.I., thus depriving them of “real-world” skills which allegedly
make it indispensable. When I first encountered A.I. plagiarism, a colleague
at the liberal arts college where I taught remarked “We [history professors]
keep telling students to slow down with A.I., but the business school is
telling them to speed up, it’ll make them more productive.” It’s easy to guess
which side of this mixed message young people take to heart: the one with
productivity and a financial bottom line in its corner. Documented atrophy of
thought and written expression should surprise no one.[[11]]()

Because A.I. magnifies our tendency to believe anything, or nothing, by
“hallucinating” alternative realities and generating infinite counterfactual
worlds. It builds on the post-truth culture enabled by the Internet. That
culture thrives on conspiracies: 9-11 was “an inside job,” climate change is a
hoax, vaccines don’t work, school shootings were staged by a “deep state”
trying to enslave us, legitimate elections were “rigged.”[[12]]() Big lies
have become mainstream discourse.

Because, in my classroom, facts are now up for grabs. When students show me an
A.I. deepfake or Instagram post as “evidence,” or ask questions such as “you
think astronauts really walked on the moon?,” I realize we don’t share the
same reality. When facts are fungible, history becomes unteachable.

Because Americans’ awareness of history is built on unstable foundations:
movies, television shows, TV news. A large majority see history as “little
more than an assemblage of names, dates, and events,” according to a recent
American Historical Association survey. Less than a third read books on
history. College courses rate dead last as a source for the general-public’s
historical understanding.[[13]]()Young people are far more likely to turn to
YouTube than a library or university for history education.

Because education professor Sam Wineburg misstated the problem when he called
historical thinking an “unnatural act.”[[14]]() History, as I know it,
involves making arguments from primary- and secondary-sources. Those sources
are almost always textual. Arguments require objectivity, an ability to detach
from one’s own identity and imagine how historical actors behaved and thought.
They necessitate an awareness for context, contingency, chronology, and
causation. Arguments must be revised or scrapped in the face of contradictory
evidence and better arguments. The primary vehicle for history scholarship is
a book-length monograph. History’s disciplinary approach lacks relevance for
what used to be called an educated citizenry. It’s not unnatural; it’s
archaic.

My assertion of history’s death differs from a largely discredited claim by
political theorist Francis Fukuyama. Near the end of the Cold War, Fukuyama
saw “the end of history” in the triumph of Western democracy over
authoritarianism. He believed that history’s motive force, its dialectic,
ceased along with the Soviet Union. Fukuyama focused on processes, not
method.[[15]]() It’s the latter that has died, the actual guts of the
discipline.

An example suggests how much we’ve atrophied. During the Cuban Missile Crisis
of 1962, President John F. Kennedy spoke with advisors about a work of history
he had read several months earlier, Barbara Tuchman’s analysis of the outbreak
of WWI, _The Guns of August_. The book described European leaders’
straitjacketed militaristic thinking and how it led them to catastrophe.
Kennedy said “I am not going to follow a course that will allow anyone to
write a comparable book about this time, [ titled] _The Missiles of October_.
If anyone is around to write after this, they are going to understand that we
made every effort to find peace and every effort to give our adversary room to
move.” Tuchman won a Pulitzer-Prize for _Guns_ , in part because of Kennedy’s
invocation. It was a Book of the Month Club read, which is itself an
artifact.[[16]]() One can hardly imagine a work of history having a comparable
impact on leaders or the public today.

Why keep teaching it, then? I still love history, and, for me, loving it
matters. My best teaching moments, when it seems I’ve conjured the past into
our classroom for students to see, touch, smell, provide compensation. That’s
my existential payoff. As a new school year approaches, I still chase those
moments.

Professionalism matters, too: working to know and understand my students;
sweating lesson plans, assessments, field trips, guest speakers; keeping
current in my subject; showing up in dress code; maintaining collegiality;
communicating with parents and administrators; attending office hours;
commenting thoughtfully on student work; configuring my classroom. I take
pride in doing the job well.

Personal rationales don’t address the larger question, though, which is what
happens to a society cut off from historical insight, one that has chosen not
to know itself?

On that score, at least, Fukuyama rightly foresaw “the end of history will be
a very sad time.”[[17]]() He thought post-history society would lose an
ideological perspective that gave life meaning. As I see it, without history,
we’re deracinated, vulnerable to demagogues and fundamentalism, and,
ultimately, we face a similar crisis of meaning. Contemplating that, I’m happy
to go back to my classroom this fall and carry on as though history still
lived.
